01.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives and Rabbi Yohanan
01.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized an orphans' cow for a debt and Rabbi Yohanan approved, but Reish Lakish ordered it returned.
01.turn: Reish Lakish overruled Rabbi Yohanan's approval, and the relatives went back to complain.
01.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he could do nothing because his peer disagreed with him.
01.summary: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan seized a cow belonging to orphans, whose father owed them money. Rabbi Yohanan said they had seized it properly, but Reish Lakish told them to give it back. When they returned to Rabbi Yohanan, he said he could not help, since his equal disagreed with him.

02.actor: Rav Nahman and the daughter of his relative
02.event: Purchasers of a dead woman's marriage-contract rights claimed the money from her daughter, and Rav Nahman suggested a way for the daughter to avoid paying.
02.turn: Rav Nahman's advice: forgive her father's marriage-contract debt so she could inherit it from him.
02.outcome: The daughter heard this, went and forgave her father's obligation as advised.
02.summary: A relative of Rav Nahman sold her marriage contract rights, was divorced and then died. The buyers claimed the money from her daughter. Rav Nahman asked aloud whether no one would advise the girl to forgive her father's obligation and then inherit from him. She heard and did exactly that.

03.actor: A couple, their minor daughter, and the father's relative
03.event: A couple disagreed over whom to marry their minor daughter to; the father yielded to the mother's relative, but during the festive meal his own relative came up to the roof and betrothed her.
03.turn: The father's relative betrothed the girl in the middle of the meal.
03.outcome: The passage itself ends with the betrothal; whether it is valid is only addressed in the following discussion (presumed not valid).
03.summary: A father wanted to marry off his minor daughter to his relative and the mother to hers. Under pressure the father agreed to the mother's relative. While they were eating and drinking, the father's relative came onto the roof and betrothed her. The Gemara then assumes the father did not desire this betrothal.
03.missing: The legal outcome of the betrothal is stated only in the surrounding discussion.

04.event: Mar Zutra compelled a rebellious wife who said she was disgusted with her husband to stay with him.
04.turn: A son, Rabbi Hanina of Sura, was born of this couple, which suggests coercion can bring blessing.
04.outcome: The Gemara rejects this as a precedent: the good result was due to heavenly assistance.
04.summary: A woman rebelled against her husband, saying she was disgusted with him, and Mar Zutra forced her to stay. From that couple came Rabbi Hanina of Sura. The Gemara says this proves nothing general; it happened by heavenly help.

05.actor: A man who sold his mother's marriage contract rights, and Rami bar Hama and Rava
05.event: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract, saying he would not reimburse if she objected; she died without objecting, then he himself contested the sale.
05.turn: Rami bar Hama thought he stands in his mother's place and can object; Rava challenged this.
05.outcome: Rava argued he guaranteed against his own objections too; the passage is essentially a legal exchange.
05.summary: A man sold his mother's marriage contract rights on the condition that he would not compensate if she objected. She died having never objected, and he came and contested the sale. Rami bar Hama thought he could object as her proxy, but Rava answered that he had guaranteed the sale against his own objections.
05.missing: No judgment is explicitly delivered; it is framed as a legal argument.

06.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
06.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to test whether the son would become angry.
06.turn: The Gemara asks whether this tempted the son to sin and violated the ban on destruction.
06.outcome: The outcome of the test is not stated; the following discussion only defends the act's permissibility.
06.summary: Rav Huna decided to tear silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would get angry. The Gemara then raises objections that this might make the son sin or destroy property, and answers them. How Rabba actually reacted is never told.

07.actor: A man who fell into the Great Cistern (per Rabbi Meir)
07.event: Rabbi Meir cites an incident of a man falling into the Great Cistern, which the Sages say is a miracle not to be used for halakha.
07.turn: Debate over whether surviving without eating, drinking or sleeping makes it miraculous.
07.outcome: The incident itself is only gestured at; the passage is about whether it counts as miraculous.
07.summary: Rabbi Meir mentions an incident of a man who fell into the Great Cistern and survived. The Sages answer that one does not cite miraculous events. The Gemara then debates what exactly was miraculous about the case.
07.missing: The incident's actual details are not told in the text shown.

08.actor: Rami bar Hama, Mar Ukva, Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman
08.event: Their mother wrote her property to Rami in the morning and to Mar Ukva in the evening, and each brother got a different judge to confirm his claim.
08.turn: Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman, who had ruled differently, confronted each other about their reasons.
08.outcome: Rav Nahman rejected Rav Sheshet's reasoning, saying he himself is a judge and Rav Sheshet is not, and that Rav Sheshet's reasoning was originally different.
08.summary: A mother gave her property by deed to Rami bar Hama in the morning and to his brother Mar Ukva in the evening. Rami won before Rav Sheshet and Mar Ukva won before Rav Nahman. When Rav Sheshet challenged Rav Nahman, they argued over whose reasoning held up, and Rav Nahman insisted his was the judge's discretion while Rav Sheshet was no judge.

09.actor: A launderer who visited Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi every day
09.event: After a Divine Voice promised the World-to-Come to all who attended Rabbi's funeral, the launderer, who had not come that day, heard of the death and the promise.
09.turn: Overcome with grief, he climbed to the roof and fell to his death.
09.outcome: A Divine Voice declared that this launderer too is destined for the World-to-Come.
09.summary: On the day of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's funeral a Divine Voice said all who attended would have a place in the World-to-Come. A launderer who visited Rabbi daily had not come that day. When he heard, he went up to the roof and fell to the ground and died, and a Divine Voice announced that he too was destined for the World-to-Come.

10.actor: A man who had never been married and Rav Nahman
10.event: A man came before Rav Nahman claiming he found an unobstructed opening on his wedding night.
10.turn: Rav Nahman suspected he had experience with prostitutes since he was unmarried.
10.outcome: Rav Nahman ordered him flogged with palm branches.
10.summary: A man who had not been married before told Rav Nahman that he had found his bride's opening unobstructed. Rav Nahman said to flog him with palm branches, since prostitutes are common around him, so he must have learned of the condition from experience.

11.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi if he remembered testimony; Rav Ashi said no, but after being reminded eventually remembered and testified for him.
11.turn: Rav Kahana was hesitant that he had influenced Rav Ashi's memory.
11.outcome: Rav Ashi said he was not relying on Rav Kahana but had made an effort and truly remembered.
11.summary: Rav Ashi knew testimony relevant to Rav Kahana. At first Rav Ashi said he did not remember, but eventually he recalled it and testified. Seeing Rav Kahana doubtful about it, Rav Ashi told him he was not relying on him but had made an effort and remembered on his own.

12.event: Rav Avya came to Neharde'a and saw a man tying a bolt to a door with a reed.
12.turn: He ruled that the door may not be locked on Shabbat with such a bolt.
12.outcome: Only his ruling is given; no further events.
12.summary: Rav Avya visited Neharde'a and saw a man tying a bolt to a door with a reed. He declared that this door could not be locked on Shabbat. The text gives no reaction or aftermath.
12.missing: What the man did in response.

14.actor: The daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon and the Sages
14.event: The Sages set aside four hundred gold coins for her perfume account for a single day.
14.turn: She responded by blessing them: may you set the same for your own daughters.
14.summary: After the death of her husband, the Sages allotted Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter four hundred gold coins for her daily perfume expenses. She said to them that they should set the same for their own daughters, and they answered Amen.

15.event: Rabbi Ami cites a tumtum of Biri who was seated and torn open and then fathered seven children, as an objection to Rabbi Yehuda.
15.turn: Rabbi Yehuda's answer: check where his children came from.
15.outcome: The case is used only as an argument and the outcome is not narrated beyond the seven children.
15.summary: Rabbi Ami raised the case of a tumtum from Biri, who was seated, torn open and later fathered seven children, to challenge Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yehuda could reply that one should look into where those children came from.
15.missing: The incident is only an offhand reference within a legal challenge.

16.event: Shmuel's father posted guards over captive women and Shmuel objected; later Shmuel's own daughters were taken captive.
16.turn: The daughters left their captors outside, declared in the study hall that they were captive and pure, and were permitted to marry.
16.outcome: When the captors then came in, the permission stood, and it became clear they were Shmuel's daughters.
16.summary: Shmuel's father posted guards over captive women who had come to Neharde'a, and Shmuel questioned him; the father asked whether he would treat his own daughters so. It came true: Shmuel's daughters were captured and brought to Eretz Yisrael. They entered the study hall first and each declared she was captive and pure, and were permitted. When their captors came in, it was revealed whose daughters they were.

17.actor: A certain woman and the guard she was with
17.event: A woman, visiting her husband's grave, had intercourse with a man guarding an executed body, then suggested they disinter her husband so he could claim the guarded body was safe.
17.turn: Even in acute mourning she succumbed to temptation.
17.outcome: She removed her husband's body from its grave.
17.summary: The Rabbis' view is illustrated by an incident of a woman who removed her husband's body from the grave. She had gone to his grave, been with a man guarding a hanged body, and when that body was stolen proposed that her husband be dug up to stand in for it.
17.missing: The Aramaic only hints at the story; the details come from the translator's explanation.

18.actor: Rabbi Meir and a man who made an eiruv with onions
18.event: Rabbi Meir spent Shabbat in Ardiska and a man told him he had made an eiruv with onions in order to walk to Tiv'in.
18.turn: Rabbi Meir did not accept the onion eiruv.
18.outcome: He made the man stay within his four cubits.
18.summary: Rabbi Meir was spending Shabbat in Ardiska when a man told him he had made an eiruv of Shabbat limits with onions to reach Tiv'in. Rabbi Meir would not accept it and kept him within four cubits.

19.actor: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, and his sharecropper
19.event: The sharecropper brought a basket of fruit on Thursday instead of Friday because he had a lawsuit before Rabbi Yishmael.
19.turn: Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift, disqualified himself, and had others judge the case.
19.outcome: While the case was judged he kept thinking of ways the sharecropper could win, and concluded that bribe-takers must be even more biased.
19.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper normally brought fruit on Friday but once came on Thursday, because he had a case before the rabbi. Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and disqualified himself, and two scholars judged the case. All the while he found himself mentally arguing for the sharecropper, and reflected that if he felt this way without taking anything, bribe-takers must be far more biased.

20.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with stolen coins, and Rava
20.event: A man grabbed coins from someone, threw them to a woman washing her feet, and declared her betrothed.
20.turn: He came before Rava to ask about her status.
20.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal ineffective, since the coins were stolen and the owner presumably has not despaired of them.
20.summary: A woman was washing her feet in a basin when a man snatched coins from another person, threw them to her, and said she was betrothed to him. He asked Rava about it. Rava ruled it was not valid because the coins were not truly his, as the owner would not have given up on them.
